title: Poisson arrival sweep notes — asymmetric batching and warmup artifacts
content:
Goal:
Short notes and results from a set of Poisson-arrival workload sweeps. Trying to reproduce real-world arrival variability and measure impact on batching timeout, KV-cache behavior, and tail latency.

Hypothesis:
- Poisson arrivals (vs steady QPS) produce sporadic microbursts that change batching dynamics and increase p95/p99.
- Increasing batch_timeout reduces tail latency by letting more requests aggregate, but hurts p50 and increases median latency.
- KV cache hit-rate interacts with arrival patterns; session-affinity improves cache efficiency and reduces mean token compute.

Testbed / environment:
- Model: redwood/open-7b-quant-v2 (quantized int8 path), sequence length 512 typical prompts
- Serving: dedicated-pool-3 (2x A100-SXM4 80GB per node), runtime v0.33.1-nightly
- Client: custom loadgen run_poisson.py (scripts/loadgen/poisson-client.py), uses asyncio + jittered sleeps following Poisson process (inter-arrival exp(1/lam))
- Network: colocated client in the same region (us-west-2), measured baseline RTT ~3ms
- Batching knobs: batch_timeout_ms = [6, 12, 24]; max_batch_size = 64; concurrency per worker = 8
- KV cache: on/off via env REDWOOD_KV_CACHE=true/false; session_affinity window = [30s, 300s]
- Duration: 10 minutes warmup + 10 minutes collection per run

Commands / runner examples:
- run client: python run_poisson.py --target-rps 120 --duration 600 --seed 42 --arrival poisson --out results/poisson-rps-120.json
- orchestration: ./scripts/run_sweep.sh --rps-list 40,80,120,180 --batch-timeouts 6,12,24 --kv true,false
- server metrics: curl -s http://metrics-host:9090/api/metrics | jq '.batcher, .kv_hits' > server_metrics.json

Key measured signals:
- Achieved RPS (requests/s) from client
- Server concurrency and queue depth distribution
- p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side, request->first-token and request->last-token) in ms
- Error rate (HTTP 5xx or 429)
- Batch size distribution (percentiles)
- KV cache hit % (requests where prefix cache used)

Representative run (summary):
- Settings: target RPS = 120 (Poisson), batch_timeout = 12ms, KV cache = true, session_affinity = 300s
- Achieved RPS: 118.6 (client measured)
- Errors: 0.2% (mostly 503 transient during a single node restart)

Latency (ms):
- p50: 42 ms
- p95: 142 ms
- p99: 312 ms
- tail spike notes: occasional 600-900ms outliers correlated with single-node GC/eviction events in logs (see timestamp 2025-01-23T15:12Z)

Batching distribution:
- mean batch size: 14
- batch size p90: 28
- small batches (<4) accounted for 23% of requests (these map to microbursts)

KV cache:
- hit %: 74% overall; when session_affinity=30s this drops to ~61% and p95 increases ~12%

Comparative sweep: batch_timeout effects at target RPS=120 (Poisson)
- timeout 6ms: p50 36ms, p95 192ms, p99 420ms, mean batch size 9, small_batches 36%
- timeout 12ms: p50 42ms, p95 142ms, p99 312ms, mean batch size 14, small_batches 23%
- timeout 24ms: p50 58ms, p95 124ms, p99 260ms, mean batch size 19, small_batches 12%

Interpretation:
- Shorter timeout reduces median significantly (good for interactive latency) but increases tail a lot because more requests get shipped in small batches during microbursts, causing high per-request overheads and more variance.
- Longer timeout raises p50 but smooths p95/p99 — at 24ms we see fewer extreme tails but increased median. This aligns with expected batching tradeoff.
- The optimal timeout depends on SLAs: for p95-focused services, 12-24ms looked better; for sub-100ms median targets, 6ms helps but tail risk is high.

Poisson vs steady arrivals (same mean RPS = 120):
- Steady (fixed inter-arrival): p95 ~98ms, p99 ~190ms, mean batch size 17
- Poisson: p95 ~142ms, p99 ~312ms, mean batch size 14
- Conclusion: stochastic arrivals materially worsen tails even at same mean RPS by producing more small-batch events and occasional short-packed bursts that trigger queue contention and blocking on GPU kernel launch.

Anomalies / notes:
- Observed a consistent ~10ms gap between client-perceived latency and server first-token metric; likely client-side connection latency + serialization. Need to instrument client more precisely.
- One run showed a persistent 1% 429 spike aligned with autoscaler briefly dropping one worker; check autoscaler logs for scale-down policy.
- Batcher logs show occasional >100ms dequeue stalls when node memory pressure triggered internal GC. Correlate with node-level dmesg and kubelet OOM events.

Actionable next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Re-run with tighter node-stability: pin nodes, disable autoscaler for baseline to remove scale events (assigned to Priya)
- [ ] Add client-side synthetic jitter control to test extremes: CV (coefficient of variation) sweeps (assigned to Elliot)
- [ ] Instrument kernel startup times to confirm if long tails are kernel launch vs model forward compute
- [ ] Explore adaptive batch_timeout: dynamic increase during detected microbursts to trade p50 vs p99 automatically (prototype plan: rules in router, PR reference above)
- [ ] Run same sweep on smaller model (2.7B) to isolate model-compute vs batching overhead

Notes to self (scratch):
- For writeup include small figure: two CDFs (Poisson vs steady) highlighting rightward tail for Poisson.
- Mention integration with Redwood Optimize: could suggest a heuristic to detect arrival variance and pick batch_timeout automatically per-route.

Quick conclusions (one-liner):
- Poisson-style arrival variability increases tail latency significantly; batching timeout is an effective lever but requires SLA-aware tuning (or adaptive algorithms) to avoid median/tail tradeoffs.

Raw artifacts location:
- results/poisson-sweep-2025-01-23/ (client JSONs, server_metrics.json, batcher_logs.tar.gz)

If anyone wants to reproduce: ping me (Diego) and I will share the scripts and a short runbook.

End of notes.
